# 2.1 Romeo and Juliet

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Juliet learns Romeo is a Montague

Two lines carry Juliet's reaction, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is "O Romeo, Romeo! Wherefore art thou Romeo?" (Shakespeare 2.2.33).
"Wherefore" here does not mean "where are you Romeo", it means "Why are you
Romeo". Getting this right changes the whole line: she is not calling out for him,
she is protesting at his identity. It shows that Juliet is incredibly miserable
that the man she loves is a Montague, and it shows the "star crossed lovers"
archetype even more clearly, because the obstacle is written into his name.

The second, and more famous, is "What's in a name? That which we call a rose / By
any other word would smell as sweet" (Shakespeare 2.2.43-44). Here she expresses
that a name does not matter to her, as Romeo would be who he is regardless of
what he is called. This tells us that she is willing to love Romeo nevertheless:
she pushes the family feud away from their relationship because she thinks it
does not change anything.

Read together, the two lines are the same problem stated twice — first as
despair, then as the decision to ignore it.

## The introduction of Friar Lawrence

Friar Lawrence enters with a monologue about plants, of which the key couplet is
"Within the infant rind of this weak flower / Poison hath residence and medicine
power" (Shakespeare 2.3.22-23).

Through many lines like this one, the monologue argues that plants are not
completely good and not completely bad. That is a hint towards the poisonous vials
that Romeo and Juliet drink later on — the same substance can preserve or kill,
which is exactly what happens in the play.

It is also through this section that we are told Friar Lawrence is really
experienced with different herbs and plants. That expertise foreshadows that he
would be the one to give Juliet the suggestion to drink the vial.

## Mercutio's catalogue of women

Laura, Dido, Cleopatra, Helen and Hero are known to be extremely pretty women, but
also to have extremely tragic love stories. Dido commits suicide after Aeneas
abandons her; Cleopatra commits suicide after being defeated by Augustus; and
Hero throws herself from a tower after her lover drowned to death. The beauty is
never the point of the list — the deaths are.

Most notably, there is the reference to Thisbe. Thisbe's story is definitely
analogous to Romeo and Juliet: it starts with star crossed lovers and ends with
both committing suicide because each thought the other was dead. These references,
and especially Thisbe, foreshadow the tragic ending of Romeo and Juliet.

## Act 3 Scene 5: Juliet bids Romeo farewell

These few pages are heavy with images of light and darkness, and of death.

The two keep on referring to larks and nightingales, as larks represent the
morning and nightingales the night — so the argument about which bird they can
hear is really an argument about whether Romeo has to leave. Phrases such as
"jocund day / stands tiptoe on the misty mountain tops" (Shakespeare 3.5.9-10)
once again show that the night is retreating.

Romeo and Juliet switch sides here a lot, so pay attention to who is telling whom
to stay and who is telling whom to leave. Losing track of that is the easiest way
to misread the scene.

Eventually they bid farewell, but with another line from Romeo: "More light and
light; more dark and dark our woes!" (Shakespeare 3.5.36). That is a direct
foreshadow of what happens later in the story, as Juliet is then forced to marry
Paris. Juliet then says that "Methinks I see thee, now thou art so low, / as one
dead in the bottom of a tomb" (Shakespeare 3.5.55-56), foreshadowing again that
the day will only grow worse.

## Why Capulet is furious when Juliet rejects Paris

More than one reason can be argued. The slightly more positive one considers more
factors. Paris is said to be handsome, rich, and related to the prince, which
gives Juliet a lot more power by marrying him — so Capulet's rage can be read as
that of a father watching his daughter refuse an advantageous match rather than
purely as tyranny.

## Mercutio's "grave man" line

"Grave man" is a pun, meaning both that he is very serious and that he is on the
verge of dying. This shows us more about Mercutio's trickster personality: even
when he is going to die, he is still busy making puns about his soon-to-be death.

## Peter and the musicians at the end of Act 4 Scene 5

Act 4 Scene 5 is the scene where everyone thinks Juliet is dead, and Shakespeare
closes it with an odd conversation between Peter and the musicians. The reason
becomes clear with the historical context: Shakespearean plays at the time were
not considered classy and were for the commonfolk. The conversation appeals to
that audience, who were in similar situations to the musicians in the play.

The musicians are concerned about their payment now that Juliet has died, much
like how the audience would react given the situation, as likely none of them
were as rich as the Montagues and Capulets. The scene lets the people in the
theatre see their own concerns on stage immediately after a tragedy that belongs
entirely to the wealthy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Wherefore** | In Juliet's line, "Why are you Romeo" — not "where are you Romeo" |
| **Star crossed lovers** | The archetype Romeo and Juliet belong to, shown by Juliet's misery that the man she loves is a Montague, and paralleled in Thisbe's story |
| **Foreshadowing** | A hint at what comes later, as in Friar Lawrence's speech on plants pointing towards the vials, and the Thisbe reference pointing towards the ending |
| **Pun** | A word used in two senses at once, such as Mercutio's "grave man": very serious, and on the verge of dying |
| **Trickster** | Mercutio's personality type — still making puns about his own soon-to-be death |

# 4.1 Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Plot outline

What follows is a very general plot outline, meant merely for reference. For the
test you are expected to have much more specific knowledge than this, so use it
to fix the order of events and then go back to the novella for detail.

| Chapter | Events |
|---|---|
| 1 | Mr Utterson, a lawyer, learns from his friend Mr Enfield about a horrible incident in which a man, Mr Hyde, trampled a young girl but paid a large check when threatened by the police. |
| 2 | Utterson is troubled that one of his clients, Dr Jekyll, has made a will leaving everything to Hyde rather than to his own family. He visits Dr Lanyon, an old friend of Jekyll's, who has never heard of Mr Hyde — which leaves Utterson more concerned. Utterson then spies on the house where Hyde trampled the girl, and goes to Jekyll's house; Jekyll is absent, and a servant, Poole, treats Mr Hyde almost like a master. |
| 3 | Utterson visits Jekyll's dinner party and asks him about the matter. Jekyll will not reveal anything, saying only that he can choose to be free of Hyde whenever he likes. |
| 4 | After a year, Mr Hyde murders a respected old man, Sir Danvers Carew, a client of Utterson's. Utterson takes the police to Hyde's address, but they find nothing except the burnt-out end of a checkbook. |
| 5 | Utterson visits Jekyll, who says he is finished with Mr Hyde and shows Utterson a letter from him. Utterson's clerk, a handwriting expert, inspects it and discovers the letter was written in Jekyll's hand. |
| 6 | Jekyll is back to his old self and starts to see his friends again, but after two months he goes through a dramatic change and becomes reclusive. Lanyon tells Utterson he has had a shock that will soon kill him, and gives Utterson a letter to read when Jekyll is dead. |
| 7 | Utterson and Enfield decide to pay Jekyll a visit while walking past his old lab. Jekyll greets them, but is suddenly overtaken by terror and flees from the window. |
| 8 | Poole visits Utterson in a panic and takes him to the house. Someone has locked himself inside the lab, and the voice that comes out is Mr Hyde's. Utterson and Poole, thinking Jekyll has been murdered, break in and find Hyde's dead body on the floor along with some documents, including a letter from Jekyll containing his confession, which Utterson takes home to read. |
| 9 | The letter Lanyon asked Utterson not to open until both Lanyon and Jekyll had died. Lanyon was asked by Jekyll to fetch ingredients from Jekyll's lab for an experiment and to await a visit from a man. A man whose appearance is clearly that of Mr Hyde arrives, makes a potion and drinks it, and his body and appearance gradually warp into those of Dr Jekyll. |
| 10 | The letter containing Jekyll's "Confession". Jekyll, proposing a theory of human evil/good duality, succeeded in finding a method to separate the two. Able to transform into Mr Hyde, Jekyll gained a new life in which all his beastly instincts could be pursued. After Hyde committed crimes, Jekyll decided to stop transforming, yet one time the transformation occurred involuntarily, forcing Jekyll to confess to Lanyon in order to gain the chemicals he needed to transform back. After returning home, Hyde takes over, and Jekyll is forced to lock himself up, sending Poole out for more chemicals. The potion has lost its effectiveness, so Jekyll writes the last of his confession and then turns into Hyde forever. |

Two structural points follow from this. The final two chapters are documents, not
scenes, so the reader learns the truth after Utterson does and in written form.
And the potion failing is what makes the ending inevitable — Jekyll does not
choose to become Hyde permanently, he simply loses the means to change back.

## Character analysis

**Dr Henry Jekyll** is presented as a fine Victorian gentleman: well mannered,
respected, and having a wide circle of friends. Central to the plot's progression
is his belief in a human good-versus-evil duality and his intention to separate
the two. His ability to transform into Mr Hyde allowed him to live a double life
in which he could engage in malevolent atrocities and unleash his beastly nature
with no damage to his reputation. As Jekyll gradually lost control over the
transformation process, he became increasingly isolated and depressed,
illustrating his struggle against the sinister side of his nature.

**Mr Edward Hyde** is constantly dehumanised from his first appearance in the
novel, described with terms such as "Savage", "Snarled", "Ape-like" and "Hardly
human", which illustrate his animosity and separation from civilised society.
Central to his characterisation are descriptions of his "deformed" looks, which
never specify the nature of the deformation — the vagueness is deliberate and
gives a sense of uncertainty and mystery. Throughout the story Hyde attacks two
innocent victims, the first an attack and the second a murder. He leaves an
impression of horror on other characters, perhaps indicating people's fear of
their own malicious side.

**Gabriel John Utterson** is the character through whom most of the third-person
narration takes place, slowly unveiling the truth behind Mr Hyde. His rational,
calm and objective narrative allows the reader to perceive the story
independently rather than being told what to think. He is a kind, polite
character, a respectable lawyer, and a trustworthy friend and adviser. Utterson
stimulates most of the plot's progression by investigating the matter, leading
the police to the house, and so on. The novel ends with Utterson reading the
letters left by Jekyll and Lanyon, yet his reaction is never mentioned, which
adds a mysterious atmosphere at the end.

**Hastie Lanyon**, a close friend of Jekyll, believes Jekyll's experiments are
morally objectionable and unscientific, describing them as "Unscientific
Balderdash". Being traditional and conventional, he is destroyed by what he sees:
when he witnesses Hyde's transformation into Jekyll with his own eyes, the entire
scientific world view on which his life had been built is mercilessly shattered.
The shock that such a monstrous beast lies within the gentleman deeply disgusts
Lanyon and leads to the end of his friendship with Jekyll.

**Enfield** is presented in Chapter I and helps to shape the initial impression of
Hyde.

**Sir Danvers Carew** is a well-respected, distinguished gentleman and even a
member of Parliament, characterised as a model Victorian-era gentleman. This
creates a stark contrast with his murder by Hyde, and so helps to characterise
Hyde as someone who opposes traditional Victorian values.

**Poole** is Jekyll's faithful servant. He alerts Utterson to the sudden
transformation of his master.

## Themes

### Duality

The duality of human nature is one of the most central themes of the novel. It is
presented primarily through the character of Jekyll: on the surface he is a
respectable, well-mannered Victorian-era model gentleman, conflicted by his
sinister inner desires. He wishes to be a respectable doctor following the highest
moral standards, yet yearns to engage in the most terrible atrocities of mankind.

The theme is also presented in the setting — London. There are contrasting
descriptions of areas of degradation and poverty next to wealthy ones, and the
contrast is written into a single building: the front door of Jekyll's house is
presented as having "a great air of wealthy and comfort", whereas the back door
leaves an impression of "Sordid negligence". The house is the man.

### Good versus evil

The theme of good versus evil is present throughout the story. In Jekyll's view,
"man is not truly one, but truly two". He acknowledges both his good and his evil
side, and the atrocities committed by Hyde illustrate the consequences of giving
in to one's evil side. Hyde is associated with Christian ideas about Hell and
Satan, and Jekyll repeatedly refers to him as "my devil". Through the novel it is
proposed that the inherent evil aspect of man is merely suppressed by society —
suppressed, not removed, which is why removing the suppression releases Hyde
intact.

### Reputation

The novel also contains the theme of reputation. Jekyll separated Hyde from
himself in order to experience the pleasure of unleashing animosity while
maintaining his reputation. The theme extends beyond Jekyll: during his
investigations, Utterson never announced his suspicions about Jekyll publicly,
partly to maintain his friend's reputation, despite realising Hyde's depravity.
At the end of the novel, even after Jekyll's death, Utterson says, "I would say
nothing of this paper. If your master has fled or is dead, we may at least save
his credit".

## Historic context

The novella was written in the 19th century, a period of rapid industrialisation
in Britain. The result was the hasty growth of population, from 1 million in 1800
to 6.7 million in 1900, leading to massive poverty and social gaps. This
inequality is demonstrated in the novel by the setting of London and the
contrasting descriptions of neighbourhoods — the setting is not background but
evidence of the period's divisions.

During this era the science of **physiognomy** was popular: the idea that the
study of a person's physical appearance could determine aspects of their internal
morality. This idea is clearly demonstrated in Hyde. Stevenson's portrayal of him
focuses heavily on his wicked physical appearance, supporting the theory of
physiognomy.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Duality** | The idea that human nature is double; presented in Jekyll, who is a respectable Victorian gentleman conflicted by sinister inner desires, and in the setting of London |
| **Physiognomy** | A science popular in the 19th century: the idea that the study of one's physical appearance could determine aspects about their internal morality |
| **Dehumanisation** | The technique by which Hyde is described — "Savage", "Snarled", "Ape-like", "Hardly human" — illustrating his animosity and separation from civilised society |
| **Reputation** | The theme by which Jekyll separates Hyde from himself to unleash animosity while keeping his standing, and by which Utterson stays silent to save his friend's credit |

# 4.2 The Picture of Dorian Gray

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The picture as symbol

Dorian's picture is the **Faustian bargain** of this book. He makes a deal with the
devil to preserve his beauty and instead let his picture grow old for him.

There is more than just ageing involved in the picture's transformation. The
picture first changes after Dorian leaves Sibyl, and it is noted at that point
that the picture visibly looks crueller — cruelty, not age, is what registers
first. Over time the picture grows more and more ugly, as a reflection of Dorian's
corrupting soul.

The picture agonises Dorian because it forces him to deal with the fact that he
is pretty damaged. His attitude towards it keeps shifting from chapter to
chapter: at some moments he is interested in how the picture functions, and at
other times he wants to burn the thing. Either way, the picture eventually becomes
too much for him to bear, which is why he attempts to destroy it.

Because the picture symbolises Dorian's soul, destroying it means he
simultaneously kills himself. It is worth noting that Dorian never considered
suicide — he was simply selfish enough to lead himself to it.

## Secrecy

Two details carry the theme of secrecy.

The first is **light and dark imagery**. In the later chapters, whenever Dorian
confronts his picture, it is during the night, and it is also at night that he is
usually mentally unstable. We therefore see him keep up his mask in the daytime in
front of Lord Henry and Gladys, and then go pretty insane at night. The day and
night division is the secret made visible.

The second is Dorian's growing **paranoia**. Dorian is so focused on his image in
the latter half of the book that he starts suspecting everybody of trying to
expose him. This can be seen on the page where he thinks about his valet Victor
backstabbing him. It is also quite literally expressed when Dorian kills Basil,
because Basil uncovered his secret. In certain chapters, such as Chapter 11, you
can see how important his appearance has become to him — he becomes a trend to
dress according to.

## How the corruption of Dorian's soul is expressed

The corruption is not stated but tracked, and it is tracked through several
channels at once. A strong answer names more than one.

**The painting.** Dorian's corrupting soul on a frame.

**Dialogue.** This is especially important. Lord Henry is known for speaking in
paradoxes and uses the words "crude" and "vulgar" very often, and Dorian adopts
these traits later on — the borrowed manner of speech is itself evidence of
influence. One paradox that appears to be Dorian's is: "Nowadays all the married
men live like bachelors, and all the bachelors like married men." Attribution here
is not certain, because the dialogue in the PDF is disordered, so treat the
speaker as probable rather than settled.

**The garden.** There are only a few quotes on this, but there are a few mentions
of colours fading out of things, which shows Dorian's loss of morality. The
fading-colour motif begins to occur after Dorian left Sibyl, so it is safe to
assume it is a comment on his mental state.

**Substance abuse.** Dorian takes opium, which shows that he is no longer the
innocent boy he was before and is picking up bad habits.

**Cigarettes and other motifs.** Cigarettes appear a great deal in the later
chapters. At first it is just Lord Henry recommending that Basil smoke a
cigarette, which he calls a good source of quick pleasure. Dorian smokes a lot in
his late thirties, so those chapters are worth examining. The motif is a sign that
Dorian is committing to that hedonistic lifestyle, and, like drugs, it is a bad
habit he adopted from Henry.

**Allusions, direct and indirect.** There are a lot of allusions in this book that
tell a bad ending. The most interesting is the allusion to Narcissus, and one
quote is very obvious about it: "Once, in boyish mockery of Narcissus, he had
kissed, or feigned to kiss, those painted lips that now smiled so cruelly at him."
Dorian is compared to Narcissus, and like the self-obsession that killed
Narcissus, Dorian's obsession with his appearance kills his soul. There are more
allusions, such as the one to Romeo and Juliet for Dorian and Sibyl.

**Rhetorical questions and thoughts.** Dorian's thoughts are morally unacceptable
by the end of the book. He starts victim blaming a lot, especially towards Basil,
and often frames himself as the victim. There is also the moment where he calls
Sibyl a martyr, which shows how selfish he is.

**Actions.** Dorian blackmails Alan Campbell and drives a number of young men to
suicide.

## Escapism

Escapism carries a lot of symbols, and it explains material that otherwise looks
inert. Chapter 11 is extremely dry, and the whole point of it is that Dorian is
trying to escape the truth that he is a bad person by reading a book. That entire
chapter, plus the symbolism of the book given to him by Lord Henry, is about
escapism.

Dorian also tries to redeem himself a lot in the last two chapters. Frankly, it is
useless, but it is very interesting to watch him bring up people like Hetty Merton,
whom he essentially sees as a replacement for Sibyl Vane. It is important to note
that he is using these characters and these actions to gaslight himself into
thinking he is redeemable.

Even so, it is obvious that he is never actually improving, and the pattern is
established early. He starts to "redeem" himself as early as the night he left
Sibyl Vane — but that was because he could not stand his ugly portrait, and the
next day he woke up really relaxed and lazy, which showed that he never cared in
the first place. Later he tries to claim he is getting better through his
attitude towards Hetty, but this so-called improvement is just him ghosting her,
which shows nothing in reality.

Substance abuse belongs here too: Dorian takes drugs and smokes to distract
himself from his agony. There is a very specific description in the chapter before
he visits the opium den, where he stares at a box a great deal, hinting at his
substance abuse. One reading of this is that Dorian has exceeded Lord Henry and
become his own bad person — worse than Henry, because he has taken all the bad
things from Henry and has more of his own besides.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Faustian bargain** | The deal Dorian makes with the devil to preserve his beauty and let his picture grow old for him; the picture is that bargain in the book |
| **Paradox** | Lord Henry's characteristic manner of speech, which Dorian adopts later on |
| **Motif** | A recurring detail, such as cigarettes, fading colours, or substance abuse, that tracks Dorian's commitment to a hedonistic lifestyle |
| **Allusion** | A reference to another story, such as the allusion to Narcissus, whose self-obsession parallels Dorian's obsession with his appearance, or to Romeo and Juliet for Dorian and Sibyl |
| **Escapism** | Dorian's attempts to escape the truth about himself, through the book Lord Henry gives him, through drugs and cigarettes, and through false attempts at redemption |

# 5.1 Marginalisation in Of Mice and Men

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Candy's dog

There are two parts to this event that are important.

The first is what it tells us about Candy. As Candy himself says, his dog reflects
his character: Candy sees himself in his dog because he feels old and replaceable.
This is useful for analysing Candy, because it shows his insecurities and gives
more perspective on how he is marginalised — the dog is shot for being past use,
which is precisely what Candy fears about himself.

The second is the parallel with Lennie's death. Both are killed by the same weapon,
Carlson's Luger. The difference is that Candy let Carlson kill his dog for him,
while George took matters into his own hands. The two can be connected further by
animalistic imagery, since Steinbeck frequently describes Lennie's hands as paws.

When Candy's dog is shot, Candy remarks that he should have killed his dog himself
to lessen the dog's suffering. Set that against Lennie's death and the meaning of
George's action becomes clear: George being the one to pull the trigger is
significantly better than Lennie being shot by, say, Curley. It is a sign of
George's love for Lennie and of the heaviness of the decision.

The two deaths are also connected by loneliness. Candy's dog was Candy's only
companion, and Lennie was that for George.

## Marginalised characters are not all on one platform

What is key to realise is that the marginalised characters in this book are not
all on one platform regarding their place in society. The marginalised can
marginalise others, and that is what gives these characters nuance. An answer that
sorts the cast into oppressors and victims will miss most of what Steinbeck is
doing.

## Curley's wife

Curley's wife is marginalised because of her gender, but she is still the one with
the most power compared to the other marginalised individuals, because of her
relationship with Curley.

She is very obviously marginalised in that she is never given a name. That is a
way to corroborate that her identity is ignored aside from the fact that she is
Curley's wife — in other words, she is defined by her husband.

What is also to note is her naivety. Curley's wife is at best sixteen, and we are
given the context that her marriage to Curley was the result of impulse and rage,
caused by the fact that her actions are limited as a woman.

Aside from that, Curley's wife is portrayed both negatively and somewhat
redeemingly. Because she is the one with the most authority compared to the other
marginalised characters, her blatantly racist ideas in the scene where they all
gather in Crooks's room are used to communicate that she is not entirely a victim.
She is a character of nuance: she complains about the oppression she receives as a
woman, but is also an enforcer of oppression onto others. Her cynical and
self-centred personality works both ways in analysing her place in society.

## Lennie

Lennie is marginalised because of his learning disabilities, and there are a few
things to focus on.

His disabilities give him traits resembling a child. Steinbeck characterises him
as extremely dependent and gullible, as shown in the chapter where Lennie talks
with Crooks. However, Lennie becomes a victim of his own strength, as he fails to
understand his destructive abilities and therefore inflicts harm on others.

What is interesting is that his moral compass is George. Even in the last chapter
Lennie is unaware of what he did to Curley's wife; instead he repeatedly scolds
himself by saying that George will not let him tend the rabbits. This dependency
on George is also a reason for Lennie's instability, since he turns drastically
violent and hostile at the mere thought of George being harmed — Crooks's chapter
again. His sudden rage is a looming threat throughout the book: even though
audiences are guided to be sympathetic towards Lennie, when Lennie is agitated the
audience knows the consequences will be bad.

This is mainly because Lennie's learning disabilities do not let him understand
the magnitude of his actions and hardly give him a chance to calm down. He fails
to understand most characters in this book, and as a result what seems harmless to
him could be fatal to another. This is seen in Chapter 5, where he gets angry at
the puppy for dying when it was entirely his own fault. Similarly, he only breaks
Curley's wife's neck after he gets frustrated by her reaction — which was
completely justified, because she was effectively about to die — and shakes her.
To him, it was just a way to get her to calm down and stop.

These details prove that Lennie is likely never going to fit fully into his
society, as he is alienated from others by his inability to comprehend them.
George is his only caretaker throughout the book, which is why Lennie's death is
so significant.

## Candy

Candy is very often described as helpless. His insecurities are a big part of him
because of his age and his disability, having lost a hand. He is very vulnerable,
and even though he tries to stand up for people on the ranch, his helplessness
gets the better of him and he fails. He is hopeful and supportive, but his inner
qualms control him as a character.

## Crooks

The two biggest themes about Crooks are racism and segregation, and loneliness. He
is defensive and miserable most of the time, and he is the most marginalised
character in the book. Several details show it.

First, he calls Slim "Mister Slim", a direct acknowledgement that there is a
status difference between them — the other men at the ranch never do that.
Furthermore, rarely does anyone else at the ranch call Crooks by his nickname.
Before Crooks actually appears in the book, the men at the ranch refer to him with
a racial slur. They refuse to address him properly, and because they use the slur
it is evidence that they only see him by his skin colour. The men also do not
visit Crooks's room and do not play games with him, because they automatically
separate themselves from him. The piles of books in his room and his gun
communicate his loneliness and the insecurity that results from it.

Crooks is mean to Lennie at the start of the chapter because he does not believe
in Lennie's innocence and tries to take advantage of how gullible he is. However,
frankly because of Lennie's naivety, Crooks comes to feel comfortable opening up
to him.

The racism Crooks faces is extremely harmful to his personality, as is especially
shown when he says he was only kidding about the farm. This is particularly clear
when he stops trying to assert anything after Curley's wife reminds him of his
social status. Crooks is described as without ego and without any self-esteem. His
loss of character is a testament to society's ostracising and undisguised
prejudice, which over a long period has robbed him of any self-respect or ability
to connect with those around him.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Marginalisation** | Being pushed to the edges of a society; in this book every character is marginalised for a different reason, and the marginalised can marginalise others |
| **Animalistic imagery** | Imagery likening a person to an animal, as when Steinbeck frequently describes Lennie's hands as paws, connecting him to Candy's dog |
| **Nuance (in characterisation)** | The quality Curley's wife has as a character who complains about the oppression she receives as a woman but is also an enforcer of oppression onto others |
| **Segregation** | The separation shown when the men do not visit Crooks's room or play games with him, automatically separating themselves from him |

# 7.1 Poetic Devices in the Test Poems

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The poem on the test can technically contain whatever poetic device there is, so
no list can be exhaustive. The devices below are the ones worth preparing,
because they recur in the poems studied and because they are the ones you can
reliably find under time pressure.

## Consonance, assonance and alliteration

Of this group, alliteration is probably your best bet — it is very common and easy
to spot.

Alliteration is commonly used to affect how the poem is read, through the
repeating consonant at the start of each word. In practice it can provide a
"pulse" in the writing and make whatever it is describing more memorable. It is
commonly used to make something seem more urgent, but it can also have other
emotive effects.

That range is exactly why you cannot write a stock sentence about alliteration and
reuse it. When describing alliteration, you must consider the context — the same
technique is doing a different job in an angry poem and in a tender one.

## Conceit

**Conceit** is another fancy way of saying extended metaphor, and it is a very
common device in poetry.

The best poem studied that displays the use of conceit is "Women" by Alice Walker.
In "Women", Walker compares the past generation of women before her to soldiers
during wartime, in order to show how courageous and heroic they were. Note that a
conceit is judged by what the comparison lets the poet claim: the military
vocabulary is what makes the courage of those women legible as heroism rather than
as endurance.

## Enjambment

**Enjambment** is a thought carried from one line to the next without a
syntactical break. It is extremely common in poems, because it is useful in a lot
of areas.

Enjambment can place emphasis on a certain phrase or word. It can also be used to
control the pace at which the poem is read, always for some particular goal —
which is why you should read the poem in your head first and then try to analyse
it. That is annoying, but it works.

Enjambment can also reflect the speaker's tone. The enjambment used in Langston
Hughes's "Elevator Boy" can be read as showing pauses in the speaker's voice, from
which you can extrapolate that the speaker feels more and more depressed about his
bleak job, and his bleak life.

## Allusion

Allusion is crucial to understanding some of the poems studied.

Before the test, make sure you have a decent understanding of African American
history. You do not need to memorise dates or specific names, but you should be
able to recognise whether a poem is referencing the Emancipation Proclamation or
not.

If you do find an allusion, make sure you use it in your analysis, because there
is a fat chance it will be key to whatever the speaker is asserting. A good
example of this is Langston Hughes's "The Negro Speaks of Rivers".

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Alliteration** | The repeating consonant at the start of each word, used to affect how the poem is read; it provides a "pulse" in writing and makes what it describes more memorable, commonly creating urgency but capable of other emotive effects |
| **Conceit** | Another way of saying extended metaphor; a very common device in poetry, as in Alice Walker's "Women" |
| **Enjambment** | A thought running from one line to the next without a syntactical break; it can emphasise a word or phrase, control the pace of reading, and reflect the speaker's tone |
| **Allusion** | A reference within a poem to another text or historical event, such as the Emancipation Proclamation; if you find one, use it, as it is likely key to what the speaker is asserting |

# 7.2 Choosing Verbs for Poetry Analysis

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The trick is to pick your verbs well

The verb in an analytical sentence is the part that claims what the poet is doing,
so it has to fit the device you are writing about. A verb that is impressive in
one position is wrong in another. In one paragraph response, "dissect" was used
as the verb and did not really fit, because it sounded too "introductory
paragraph"-ish.

It is not great to sound repetitive, but it sounds awkward if you use the wrong
word in the wrong context, and that is often more hurtful to your writing than
repetition is. Given the choice between a repeated accurate verb and a fresh
inaccurate one, take the accurate one.

The working rule is to pick words that can describe whatever poetic device is
being used.

## Verbs to avoid

Avoid using words like "utilizes", "explains" and "relates" in your writing. They
might pass the first time, but not the second — a marker will tolerate one, and
then notice that you have no other way of saying it.

## Do not overreach for sophistication

Do not get too caught up in sounding smart. Sometimes a simple "conveys" or
"illustrates" is not going to hurt, and in fact will make your writing more
concise. Teachers like concision more than fancy writing that goes on for too
long.

| Do | Do not |
|---|---|
| Pick a verb that describes the specific device being analysed | Reach for a verb because it sounds impressive |
| Use "conveys" or "illustrates" where they are accurate | Lean on "utilizes", "explains" or "relates" |
| Accept some repetition to stay accurate | Use the wrong word in the wrong context to avoid repeating |
| Write concisely | Write at length to sound sophisticated |

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Concision** | Writing that says the thing without going on too long; teachers prefer it to fancy writing that goes on for too long |

# 7.3 Revising Of Mice and Men for the Test

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Where the novel is tested

Of Mice and Men is important in the lexis list section, so make sure you
understand the key symbols in the book. The earlier study guide on the novel is
the place to revise them from.

The likely focus of the questions is marginalisation and the American Dream, so
prepare those two before anything else.

## Writing about marginalisation

When discussing marginalisation, mention different characters. Every character in
Of Mice and Men is marginalised for different reasons, so review the differences
between each person, and review how each fits under the historical context. A
response that treats marginalisation as one condition shared equally by everyone
will not show either of those things.

The pattern to follow is a chain that runs from the personal circumstance to the
historical situation to what the character therefore wants. Candy is the clearest
example. He feels marginalised because of his age and his disability. He does not
spend time with, say, George or Slim, because he is disabled, so he only has his
dog. The marginalisation directed at him makes sense given that he is a migrant
worker: given that Candy is not even able to do basic labour, his job at the ranch
is really unstable. That instability is what makes the farm attractive to him — he
is drawn to it because of its stability and the hope of joining a community there.

Note how the last step connects marginalisation to the American Dream. Candy's
interest in the farm is not sentimentality; it follows directly from the
precariousness of his position as a disabled migrant worker.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Lexis list section** | The section of the test in which Of Mice and Men is important; it requires you to understand the key symbols in the book |
| **Marginalisation** | The condition each character in the novel experiences for a different reason, which must be linked to how it fits under the historical context — for Candy, his age, his disability, and the instability of a migrant worker's job |

# 7.4 Historical Context for the Poetry Unit

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What to be familiar with

Alongside African American history, you should also be familiar with the **Harlem
Renaissance**, since a lot of the poems studied come from that period. Make sure
you have a good understanding of Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston and Countee
Cullen.

## Why it matters even though it is not marked

It is not necessary that you mention historical context in your analysis. Knowing
more about the author and the time period will nonetheless certainly help you
understand their poems, and that understanding is what the analysis is graded on.
The context works on you before you write, not in the answer itself.

The practical way to build it is not to memorise biography. Try reading one or two
poems by each of these writers and get a grasp on their writing styles — Langston
Hughes in particular has a really obvious writing style, which makes his poems a
sensible place to start.

## Keywords

# 8.1 Reading Graphic Novels

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Start with composition

Consider composition first. Graphic novels usually use powerful composition to
balance out their storytelling so that it is more impactful — the arrangement of
the page is doing work that the words are not.

Failing that, consider movement within the panels. Ask from what view we are
looking, and how the "camera" moves from panel to panel. Both questions give you
something concrete to analyse instead of describing what happens in the story.

## Composition and movement: Maus

A page from Maus shows both at once. It begins with Art Spiegelman drawing, with
flies swirling around him, and we are not really sure why. The main focus in these
first four panels is his deteriorating mental state and how he is overwhelmed by
the workload coming from the publication of Maus I.

The panels then gradually pan out and move downwards, until we reach an impactful
panel of Spiegelman and the dead bodies — so the "camera" movement is what delivers
the revelation, and the flies are explained retrospectively.

Composition is also cleverly used here through the imbalance between Spiegelman
and the bodies. The bodies take up half of the panel, which emphasises their
presence. More than that, the raggedly drawn bodies make the page all the more
horrific to look at.

## Graphic weight: Persepolis and the Batman comic

If you want to study **graphic weight**, Persepolis is your best shot. Several
panels use graphic weight to show oppression. You could mention how the veils the
women wore were pitch black in the graphic novel: in a lot of her panels, Satrapi
uses those black veils to show how the veil oppressed her individuality and her
identity as a woman. Because black dominates whatever it sits in, the veil takes
over the panel in the same way it takes over the woman's visible identity.

The Batman comic shows graphic weight as well. In the panel in question, graphic
weight is used to give the man in the close-up — Bruce Wayne, judging by the
composition — a three-dimensional countenance. If you want to sound even more
knowledgeable, you can analyse the cold colours on one side of his face and the
slightly warmer colours on the other. The strong use of graphic weight in this
panel portrays Bruce as a mysterious person, and also shows that he is being very
serious here.

It is also interesting that the officer beside him, apparently Jim Gordon, turns
his head so that he loses more of his facial features and is left in the dark.
That forces our attention to centre on Bruce's complex expression as he explains
that Gordon is underestimating the ability of his adversary to evade the law.

## Onomatopoeia: Peter Kuper

Peter Kuper draws onomatopoeia to indicate what is happening, and the sound
effects carry action that is never shown. From two such panels we can easily tell
how Grete comes through the door: she slowly opens the door to check whether
Gregor is still out there, then grabs the newspaper holding Gregor's food and
throws it on the floor immediately, then slams the door and locks it up again.

From this combination of text and visual choices we can easily tell that Grete is
still terrified of her brother and repulsed by him, and cannot stand the sight of
him. Look out for examples like this — the sound words are evidence about a
character's feelings, not just noise.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Composition** | The arrangement of a panel or page; graphic novels use powerful composition to balance out their storytelling so that it is more impactful, as in the imbalance between Spiegelman and the bodies in Maus |
| **Movement within the panels** | Where the "camera" is and how it moves — panning out and downwards across a Maus page to reach the panel of the dead bodies |
| **Graphic weight** | The visual heaviness of dark areas in a panel, used in Persepolis to show oppression through pitch-black veils, and in the Batman comic to give a face three-dimensional depth and leave another character in the dark |
| **Onomatopoeia** | Drawn sound words, as in Peter Kuper's panels, that let the reader tell exactly what is happening and what a character feels |

# 9.1 Organising Analysis Paragraphs

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Choose the most important devices

A tip when writing analysis is always to check what the most important devices to
analyse are, before committing to any of them.

Take Malala's speech to the UN. There are several rhetorical devices she uses,
such as imagery and repetition. But if you concentrate your analysis on three
lines of repetition, compared with the whole speech, you are going to get points
off. The reason is that rhetoric accounts for the entire delivery, and a snippet
of a speech usually cannot demonstrate what the entire purpose of the speech is.

The test of a device, then, is not whether you can find it but whether it is doing
work across the piece.

## Pitching the thesis at the right width

When organising thesis statements, it is most important to clarify what choice is
involved in the device you are going to analyse.

It is important not to keep this narrow, though. You need to describe what is
being demonstrated, but keep it free as to how it is demonstrated. Otherwise the
thesis commits you to one example and leaves your body paragraphs nothing to do.

Say you are analysing diction. You could mention what connotation the diction has
and for what effect, while still leaving yourself free in your body paragraphs to
analyse the different diction choices there are. Diction could be used when the
speaker addresses her audience, or when the speaker describes a scenario — two
quite different uses, both of which your thesis should be able to cover. Written
this way, the thesis lets you address nuance in your analysis while also keeping
your transitions smooth.

## Deciding what to analyse first

When you are choosing what to analyse first, you also need to keep transitions in
mind. If your order can fit the context of the rhetoric you are analysing, that
works even better, because the essay then moves the way the text moves.

If you were writing analysis on MLK's Letter from Birmingham Jail, for instance,
it would be good to organise your points of analysis around what MLK himself
transitions from. He begins by explaining his protests and how they are harmless,
and then moves to admonishing his intended audience — whom he suggests are the
"white moderate" — for their incompetence or blatant refusal to help. An essay
ordered along that line needs almost no artificial transitions, because the shift
between its sections is the shift in the source.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Rhetoric** | The entire delivery of a speech; because it accounts for the whole delivery, a snippet usually cannot demonstrate the entire purpose of the speech |
| **Thesis statement** | A statement that clarifies what choice is involved in the device you are to analyse, describing what is being demonstrated while leaving free how it is demonstrated |
| **Diction** | Word choice; analysed by naming the connotation it carries and the effect it produces, whether the speaker is addressing her audience or describing a scenario |

# 9.2 Verbs for Magic Sentences

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The **magic sentence** is the load-bearing sentence of a piece of analysis — the
thesis of the essay, and the topic sentence of each body paragraph. The verb in it
does most of the work, because it states what the speaker is doing with the device
you are about to analyse. Always remember to look verbs up so that you are
familiar with suitable ones before you sit down to write.

## Verbs worth having ready

| Verb | When it works |
|---|---|
| **Develops** | When the speaker performs some sort of buildup in their rhetoric to prove their argument. It also helps you organise your essay or paragraph around how the speaker develops the device you are analysing. The same goes for verbs such as *compare*, *contrast*, *narrates* and *illustrates*. |
| **Assert / Advocate** | When you want to make the speaker's stance on the topic clear. These give you a little leeway for a bit of blandness, because the words themselves do not sound as bland. |
| **Emphasise** | Simple and easy. It fits a topic sentence better than a thesis, although it will work in a thesis depending on what emphasis you mention there. |
| **Use / utilises** | For any other case, these will work in a topic sentence — just try not to repeat them. |

Notice that the choice is not decorative. *Develops* commits you to an argument
that builds, and so gives you the order of your paragraph; *assert* and *advocate*
commit you to a stance; *emphasise* commits you only to a point being stressed,
which is why it sits more comfortably in a topic sentence than in a thesis that
has to cover a whole essay.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Magic sentence** | The thesis or topic sentence of a piece of analysis, whose verb states what the speaker does with the device analysed |
| **T.S.** | Topic sentence — the magic sentence that opens a body paragraph, where *emphasise* and *use/utilises* fit better than in a thesis |

# 1.1 Myth, Archetypes and the Hero's Journey

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The twelve archetypes

An **archetype** is a recurring character type that myths return to again and again. Because the same figures keep appearing across different traditions, naming the archetype is often the fastest way into a comparison question: once you can say *this is the Ruler* or *this is the Outlaw*, you have a category that lets you set two myths side by side.

The twelve archetypes you need to be able to name are:

The Hero, the Lover, the Jester, the Everyman, the Caregiver, the Ruler, the Creator, the Innocent, the Sage, the Explorer, the Outlaw, the Magician.

The guide picks out one worked identification: **The Innocent** is the archetype of the figure who "got thrown into a box". Innocence here is not the same as goodness — it is a lack of knowledge or experience, which is exactly what makes the figure vulnerable to being shut away.

## Comparing the three myths

One of the set revision questions is: *What are the similarities and differences between the three myths we learned?* The traditions the guide names for this comparison are **Norse** and **Greek**. Work through the comparison with the archetypes above and the four functions below as your headings — they give you a structure that applies to any myth, so you are not left hunting for points of contact.

## The four functions of myth

Myths are not only stories; each one does work for the society that tells it. The guide sets out four functions, and asks what relationship each has with the myths you have studied.

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Metaphysical** | Teaches people about a society's spiritual systems |
| **Cosmological** | Explains why the world is that way |
| **Sociological** | Shows cultural values and teaches people how to be in a society |
| **Pedagogical** | The fourth function named in the question |

Note the division of labour between the first three. The metaphysical function points at what lies beyond the visible world, the cosmological function accounts for the visible world itself, and the sociological function turns outward to the people living in it. That is why a single myth can be read three ways without contradiction: the same story can explain where thunder comes from *and* tell a listener how a good member of the society behaves.

The guide names the pedagogical function in the question but does not supply a definition for it, so treat that one as a term to check with your teacher rather than a definition to memorise.

## The events of the hero's journey

The hero's journey is the pattern of events a mythic hero passes through. The guide lists them in this order:

1. Hero of the known world
2. Call to adventure
3. The threshold
4. Road of trials
5. The god figure
6. The boon
7. Return
8. Changed world

The shape is circular, and that is the point. The hero begins in the known world and ends by returning to it — but the last stage is a *changed* world, not the original one. What makes the return meaningful is **the boon**: the thing won on the road of trials and brought back. Crossing **the threshold** marks the point of no return between the known world and the world of the trials, which is why it is listed as an event in its own right rather than as scenery.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Archetype** | A recurring character type in myths; the twelve are the Hero, Lover, Jester, Everyman, Caregiver, Ruler, Creator, Innocent, Sage, Explorer, Outlaw and Magician |
| **The Innocent** | The archetype identified in the guide as the figure who "got thrown into a box" |
| **Metaphysical** | Teach people about a society's spiritual systems |
| **Cosmological** | Explain why the world is that way |
| **Sociological** | Show cultural values and teach people how to be in a society |
| **The threshold** | The stage of the hero's journey between the known world and the road of trials |
| **The boon** | The stage of the hero's journey at which the hero gains what will be carried back |

# 1.2 Reading Poetry: TPCASTT and the Sonnet

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What TPCASTT stands for

**TPCASTT** is the annotation routine for working through a poem. Each letter is a pass over the text, and the order matters: you move from the surface of the poem to its meaning, and only name the theme once the earlier steps have given you the evidence for it.

| Letter | Step | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| T | **Title** | Interactive vs naming titles |
| P | **Paraphrase** | Stanza, couplet, and so on |
| C | **Connotation** | Figurative language |
| A | **Attitude** | Tone |
| S | **Shift** | Where does it change, and what changes? |
| T | **Title** | Has the meaning of the title changed? |
| T | **Theme** | What is the overall theme? (1 to 2 words) |

The two Ts at either end are the reason the routine works. You read the title first with no context, and then read it again at the end — the gap between those two readings is often the poem's whole argument. A title that looked like a plain **naming title** on the first pass may turn out to be doing something quite different once you have found the shift.

Two practical points. **Paraphrase** means restating the poem section by section — stanza, couplet — in your own words, so it is a check that you have actually understood the literal sense before you start interpreting. And the theme should come out as **one to two words**, not a sentence: if you cannot compress it that far, you have probably written a summary rather than a theme.

## The sonnet

A **sonnet** has a fixed shape, and knowing that shape tells you where to look for the argument.

| Feature | Sonnet |
|---|---|
| Length | 14 lines |
| Rhyme scheme | ABAB CDCD EFEF GG |
| Pattern | The last 2 lines are a couplet; the first line often works as a title; 12 lines set up the idea |

The rhyme scheme and the pattern are two descriptions of the same thing. The ABAB CDCD EFEF section is the twelve lines that **set up the idea**, and the GG is the closing **couplet** — the two lines that rhyme with each other and with nothing else, which is what makes them land as a conclusion. When you run TPCASTT on a sonnet, the couplet is the first place to check for the **shift**, and the first line is the first place to check for the poem's working title.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TPCASTT** | Title, Paraphrase, Connotation, Attitude, Shift, Title, Theme |
| **Title (first pass)** | Interactive vs naming titles |
| **Paraphrase** | Restating the poem by unit — stanza, couplet, and so on |
| **Connotation** | Figurative language |
| **Attitude** | Tone |
| **Shift** | Where the poem changes, and what changes |
| **Title (second pass)** | Whether the meaning of the title has changed |
| **Theme** | The overall theme, given in 1 to 2 words |
| **Sonnet** | A 14-line poem rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in which the last 2 lines are a couplet, the first line often works as a title, and 12 lines set up the idea |

# 2.1 Romeo and Juliet

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Act 1

**Scene 1.** A street fight breaks out between the servants of the rivalling families, the Capulets and the Montagues. Prince Escalus intervenes and declares that further breaches of the peace will be punished by death. That decree is worth marking: it is the reason a later brawl cannot simply be forgiven, and it is what makes banishment the sentence in Act 3.

**Scene 2.** Paris asks Lord Capulet to marry his daughter Juliet. Capulet invites Paris to the Capulet party, hoping that Juliet will meet him.

**Scene 3.** Lady Capulet and the Nurse discuss Juliet's age and marriage to Paris. Juliet is hesitant but agrees to consider him.

**Scene 4.** Romeo, Benvolio and Mercutio set off to the Capulet party in disguise. Mercutio tells Romeo the story of Queen Mab to comfort him.

**Scene 5.** At the Capulet feast, Romeo and Juliet fall in love the moment they meet. Lord Capulet and his nephew Tybalt recognised Romeo but were forced to stay down due to the Prince's orders. On the other side, Romeo and Juliet were both shocked to discover they belong to rivalling families. The scene therefore ends with both halves of the tragedy already in place — Tybalt's grudge held in check only by the Prince's decree, and a love that both lovers already know is impossible.

## Act 2

**Scene 1.** Romeo sneaks away while Mercutio and Benvolio tease him about Rosaline.

**Scene 3.** Romeo visits Friar Laurence, who agrees to help them marry, believing it will end the feud. His motive matters for any question about responsibility: the Friar is not indulging the lovers but acting on a political calculation about the feud.

**Scene 4.** Benvolio and Mercutio discuss Romeo's love life, and it is revealed that a threatening message has been received from Tybalt. The Nurse arrives, and Romeo gives her a message for Juliet regarding their wedding plans.

**Scene 5.** Juliet waits impatiently for the Nurse to return with news from Romeo. The Nurse finally arrives and reveals the wedding details.

**Scene 6.** Romeo and Friar Laurence wait for Juliet's arrival. Friar Laurence expresses his worry and warned Romeo of love. Juliet showed up and they were led to the church to get married in secret.

## Act 3

**Scene 1.** A confrontation between Mercutio and Tybalt leads to Mercutio's death. In rage, Romeo kills Tybalt and is banished from Verona.

**Scene 2.** The Nurse informs Juliet of Tybalt's death and Romeo's banishment. She is heartbroken but also angry at Romeo for his actions.

**Scene 3.** Friar Laurence informs Romeo of his banishment. Romeo is distraught but the Friar advises him to visit Juliet before leaving.

**Scene 4.** Lord Capulet decides that Juliet will marry Paris in a few days, unaware of her secret marriage to Romeo.

**Scene 5.** Romeo and Juliet spent the night together. In the morning, Romeo leaves. Lady Capulet tells Juliet about the arranged marriage. Juliet strongly refuses and was left in distress.

## Act 4

**Scene 1.** Juliet visits Friar Laurence for help. He gives her a potion that will fake her as dead for 42 hours to escape her marriage to Paris.

**Scene 2.** The Capulet household prepares for the wedding. Juliet pretends to comply with her parents' wishes.

**Scene 4.** The Capulets prepare for the wedding, oblivious to Juliet's plan. Everyone was delighted.

**Scene 5.** The Nurse finds Juliet lying "dead". The family mourns, and the wedding turns into a funeral.

## Act 5

**Scene 1.** Romeo, unaware of Juliet's faked death, hears of her death and buys a poison to join her in death.

**Scene 2.** Friar Laurence learns that Romeo did not receive his message about the plan. He rushes to the Capulet tomb.

**Scene 3.** In the tomb, Romeo encounters Paris, whom he kills. He then drank the poison and dies beside Juliet. When Juliet awakens and finds Romeo dead, she kills herself with his dagger. The families discover the tragedy and agree to end their feud.

The ending closes the circle opened in Act 1 Scene 1: the feud that began the play with a street brawl is ended only by the deaths of the two children caught in it.

## Figurative language and literary devices in the text

**Simile** — a comparison using *like* or *as*.

> "Is love a tender thing? It is too rough, Too rude, too boisterous, and it pricks like thorn." (I. iv. 25)

Spoken by Romeo, depicting his harsh and harmful love experience, the injuries formed from a thorn when it pricks the skin. The comparison is doing analytical work rather than decoration: Romeo answers his own question about whether love is tender by choosing an image that draws blood.

**Comparison** — the play's best-known example needs no *like* or *as*:

> "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the East, and Juliet is the sun." (III. i. 142)

This compares Juliet's beauty to the radiant and glorious sun.

**Foreshadowing** — the ill-fated double suicide of the young lovers was foreshadowed through several predictions and moments of the play, like Friar Laurence's warnings of love and Juliet's premonition of her death. This is why the Friar's worry in Act 2 Scene 6 is worth quoting in an essay: it reads as caution on a first pass and as prophecy on a second.

**Dramatic irony** — when the audience or reader knows more than the characters.

> "O serpent heart, hid with a flow'ring face! Did ever dragon keep so fair a cave? Beautiful tyrant, fiend angelical!" (III. ii. 79-81)

Spoken by Juliet when Romeo killed Tybalt, to express her contrasting mix of emotions of love and betrayal from Romeo's actions, meanwhile showing the difference between Romeo's murderous actions and his seemingly harmless demeanour. Every image in the three lines is a pair of opposites bolted together — serpent and flower, dragon and fair cave, tyrant and beautiful, fiend and angelical — which is how the language itself carries the split she is describing.

**Monologue** — a long speech by a character in a play, film, or other dramatic work. It reveals the character's inner emotions to the audience or other characters. In the play, monologues are often used to show characters grappling with difficult choices, expressing strong feelings, or reflecting on events in the story.

> "O Romeo, Romeo! wherefore art thou Romeo? Deny thy father and refuse thy name; Or, if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love, And I'll no longer be a Capulet." (II. ii)

In this monologue, Juliet expresses her frustration with Romeo's family name, which keeps them apart, and her willingness to give up her own name for love.

## Writing comparisons

When a question asks you to write about a comparison in the text, work in this order:

1. **Introduce and quote from the text.** Set the quotation up, then give it.
2. **Identify what is compared with what.** Name both halves — Romeo's love and the thorn; Juliet and the sun.
3. **Explain what the explicit purpose of the comparison is.** Say what the writer is using it to achieve.
4. **Use your own words to clarify the meaning.** Do not leave the quotation to speak for itself.

Step 4 is the one most often skipped, and it is the one that separates a paraphrase from an analysis: if every sentence of your explanation could have been written by someone who had only read the quotation, you have not yet clarified anything.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Simile** | Comparison using *like* or *as* |
| **Foreshadowing** | Predictions and moments earlier in a play that point towards a later event, as the lovers' double suicide is foreshadowed by Friar Laurence's warnings of love and Juliet's premonition of her death |
| **Dramatic irony** | When the audience or reader knows more than the characters |
| **Monologue** | A long speech by a character in a play, film, or other dramatic work; it reveals the character's inner emotions to the audience or other characters |

# 4.1 Short Stories: Perspective, Theme and Conflict

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Perspective and its pronouns

The narrative **perspective** of a story is identified by the pronouns the narrator uses, so this is one of the few things in literature you can settle by looking rather than by arguing.

| Perspective | Pronouns |
|---|---|
| **1st person** | I |
| **2nd person** | You |
| **3rd person** | He, She, It |

The set example is the short story **"Bread"**, which is written in the **2nd person**. That is the rarest of the three, which is precisely why it is the one likely to be asked: a story addressed to *you* puts the reader inside the situation instead of leaving them watching it.

## Internal and external conflict

Two of the set stories are examined through the distinction between **internal conflict** — a struggle inside a character's own mind — and **external conflict** — a struggle between the character and something outside them, such as circumstances or other people. Keeping the two separate is the whole skill: a character can be losing the external struggle while winning the internal one, or the reverse.

| Story | Internal conflict | External conflict |
|---|---|---|
| **"A Pair of Silk Stockings"** | Having a dilemma of what to buy — for herself or for her children | Struggles with life; poverty |
| **"A&P"** | The choice to try and grab attention | The choice to quit the job |

In "A Pair of Silk Stockings" the two levels feed each other directly. The external conflict — being poor — is what turns an ordinary purchase into a dilemma at all; with money, choosing between herself and her children would not be a choice.

## Themes of the set stories

| Story | Themes |
|---|---|
| **"Rubber Boots"** | Escapism, family, memories, grief |
| **"Fish Cheeks"** | Family, culture, identity, food, holidays, coming of age |

The theme lists overlap on **family**, and that overlap is the natural spine for a comparison question. Beyond it the two stories pull apart: "Rubber Boots" moves backwards into memories and grief, while "Fish Cheeks" moves forwards through culture and identity into coming of age.

## Must-know vocabulary by story

The words below are the ones to have ready for each text.

| Story | Words |
|---|---|
| **Fish Cheeks** | appalling; to pluck; shabby |
| **Rubber Boots** | membrane; sovereign |
| **Silk Stockings** | consternation; faculty; gaunt; judicious; morbid; to glisten |
| **A&P** | crescent; fluorescent; juvenile delinquent; rouge; striking (adj); to fumble; to saunter; to unravel; two-piece (n) |
| **Super-Frog Saves Tokyo** | boil (n); callous; collateral; gargantuan; genuine; gigantic; inhabitant; involuntary; pending; second nature; to atrophy; to barge into somewhere; via |

Three of these are given full definitions in the guide, and they are the three to learn word for word — see the Keywords table below.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **1st person** | The perspective that uses *I* |
| **2nd person** | The perspective that uses *you*; the perspective of the short story "Bread" |
| **3rd person** | The perspective that uses *he, she, it* |
| **Internal conflict** | A struggle within a character, such as the dilemma of what to buy in "A Pair of Silk Stockings" |
| **External conflict** | A struggle between a character and outside circumstances, such as poverty in "A Pair of Silk Stockings" |
| **Sovereign** | A supreme ruler, especially a monarch |
| **Morbid** | Characterised by an unusual interest in disturbing and unpleasant subjects, especially death and disease |
| **Gargantuan** | Enormous |

# 4.2 Allusion and the Bible

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Naming a biblical allusion

One of the set questions asks you to **name an allusion to the Bible**. The guide's marking note is that *answers are correct as long as they are reasonable* — so this is not a question with one memorised answer. What you are being marked on is whether you can point to a moment in a text and show that it is pointing back at scripture. Choose an allusion you can actually explain, and say what the reference brings with it, rather than reaching for the most impressive-sounding one.

Because the question is open, the useful preparation is knowing the two halves of the Bible well enough to say which one you are alluding to.

## Old Testament and New Testament

| | Old Testament | New Testament |
|---|---|---|
| **Core narrative** | The story of creation and the history of the Jewish people (the Torah) | The story of the birth, death and resurrection of Jesus |
| **Teaching** | The messages about the coming of the messiah, which Christians see as Jesus | The stories Jesus told |
| **Other material** | Special songs, stories and history | The messages and history of the beginnings of the Church |

The relationship between the two columns is what makes the distinction worth knowing. The Old Testament carries **messages about the coming of the messiah**, and the New Testament tells the story of the figure Christians identify as that messiah — so an allusion to one half often gains its force from the other. A text that alludes to a promised deliverer is drawing on the Old Testament; a text that alludes to a death and a return is drawing on the New.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Old Testament** | The story of creation and the history of the Jewish people (the Torah); the messages about the coming of the messiah, which Christians see as Jesus; special songs, stories and history |
| **New Testament** | The story of the birth, death and resurrection of Jesus; the stories Jesus told; the messages and history of the beginnings of the Church |

# 5.1 Of Mice and Men

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Setting and key events, chapter by chapter

The novel's structure is unusually tight: six chapters, each anchored to a single location, with the last returning to the first. Learning the settings alongside the events is the quickest way to hold the whole book in your head, because in this book place and meaning move together.

| Chapter | Setting | Key event |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | The Salinas River, near Soledad, California | George and Lennie are travelling to a new ranch for work |
| **2** | The bunkhouse at the ranch | George and Lennie meet Candy, the old swamper, and the boss |
| **3** | The bunkhouse | George tells Slim about the incident in Weed where Lennie grabbed a girl's dress, causing them to flee |
| **4** | Crooks' room in the barn | Lennie visits Crooks, the African American stable hand, who is isolated due to his race |
| **5** | The barn | Lennie accidentally kills his puppy by petting it too hard |
| **6** | The Salinas River, where the story began | Lennie waits by the riverbank, imagining Aunt Clara and a giant rabbit scolding him for his mistakes |

Two patterns are worth drawing out of that table.

First, **the book returns to where it started**. Chapter 1 and Chapter 6 share a setting, the Salinas River, which frames everything in between as a single closed episode rather than an open-ended story.

Second, **Chapter 3's flashback and Chapter 5's puppy are the same event twice**. In Weed, Lennie grabbed a girl's dress and would not let go, and the two men had to flee; in the barn, Lennie pets a puppy too hard and kills it. The novel tells you what Lennie's strength does before it shows you again, so that by Chapter 5 the reader understands the pattern.

**Crooks** is the only character introduced through his separation from the others: he has his own room in the barn, and the reason given is his race. Isolation is presented as something done to him rather than something he chooses.

## The debate

The novel is assessed in part through a debate, marked against a performance rubric. Two motions are set:

- **Were the labour conditions in the United States fair?**
- **Was it mercy or murder?**

The guide's answer to the second is that it **depends on your view of morality**. That is the instruction, not an evasion of it: the question has no fixed answer, so the marks are in how clearly you state the moral position you are arguing from and how consistently you hold to it. Decide first whether you are judging the act by its intention or by its outcome, say so, and then argue from there.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Crooks** | The African American stable hand, who is isolated due to his race and has his own room in the barn |
| **Candy** | The old swamper, whom George and Lennie meet at the ranch |
| **Weed** | The place of the earlier incident, where Lennie grabbed a girl's dress, causing the two men to flee |

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The list

Forty words are set for this unit. They sit in the same issue as the summary of *A Raisin in the Sun*, and the list reflects it: a large block of the words name social forces — **segregation**, **discrimination**, **prejudice**, **lynching**, **marginalized**, **oppressive**, **poverty** — while another block names positions people take up in response to those forces: **assimilationist**, **idealist**, **entrepreneur**, **decolonization**. A third block is descriptive vocabulary for how characters speak and behave: **aloof**, **brusquely**, **gingerly**, **disapprovingly**, **feeble**, **contorted**.

That grouping is a revision aid rather than a rule. Learn them in the numbered order the guide gives, but expect the social-vocabulary block to be the one that earns marks in an essay, because those are the words that let you name what a text is doing rather than only describe it.

## Words that are easily confused

A few pairs on the list sit close enough together to be worth separating before an exam.

**Bourgeois** and **proletariat** are the two halves of the same distinction — the propertied middle class and the class that owns no property — so if you can define one you can define the other by contrast.

**Deference** and **dignity** pull in opposite directions even though both are about how a person carries themselves in front of others: deference is yielding to someone, dignity is holding your own worth.

**Derogatory** and **disapprovingly** both describe negative attitudes, but the first describes language that belittles and the second describes the manner in which something is said or done.
